query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Surface doping the near-equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive catalyst with a controlled amount of Sn will enhance low‐temperature oxidation activity, improve resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO, and increase long‐term durability without increasing platinum-group-metal use.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst containing elements such as Cu and Ni with baseline performance under transient, low-temperature, and poisoning conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a surface doping treatment with Sn (tin) onto the catalyst.
generation.conditions: Catalytic performance should be evaluated under simulated automotive exhaust conditions, particularly at low temperatures (below 150 °C), in the presence of common poisons (H2O and NO), and under accelerated aging protocols representative of a full vehicle lifetime.
generation.structural_mediator: Sn atoms placed at or near the surface active sites modify the local coordination environment, promoting enhanced OH adsorption.
generation.mechanism: Sn, as an oxyphilic element, is expected to strengthen the adsorption of OH species on the catalyst surface. This facilitates the oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons, mitigating CO poisoning and maintaining prolonged catalyst activity over operational and aging cycles.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Sn-doped catalyst is anticipated to achieve lower light-off temperatures for oxidation reactions (<150 °C), show reduced poisoning by H2O and NO, and maintain higher catalytic activity after accelerated aging tests compared to the undoped catalyst.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of the original near-equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst without Sn doping under the same exhaust and aging conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected within the operational temperature range typical of automotive exhaust (<150 °C) and may be limited by the optimal Sn doping level and stability of the surface-modified configuration under extended cyclic thermal and chemical stress.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the optimal Sn surface concentration, potential adverse interactions with other alloy constituents, and the long-term stability of the Sn-doped surface under real driving emissions conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one set with controlled Sn surface doping and one undoped control. Subject both sets to simulated automotive exhaust conditions, including low-temperature operation (<150 °C), exposure to H2O and NO, and accelerated aging cycles. Compare the changes in catalytic activity, poison resistance, and durability over time.
measurements: Light-off temperature profiles for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation
Conversion efficiency metrics for CO and hydrocarbons in the presence of H2O/NO
Activity retention after accelerated aging (e.g., number of cyclic tests)
Characterization of surface composition changes (e.g., using XPS or TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-doped catalyst does not show a statistically significant lowering in oxidation temperature, enhanced resistance to poisoning, and improved durability relative to the undoped catalyst under identical test conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

reading.lever: Surface dope the multi‐principal-element catalyst with an oxyphilic element (e.g., Sn) to promote OH adsorption and mitigate CO poisoning.
reading.why: This approach leverages established benefits from Pt surface doping to enhance poisoning resistance and durability, addressing the integrated automotive catalyst challenges.
